events.content: Bank A is facing a severe liquidity crisis and may not be able to meet all withdrawal requests. Several large corporate depositors are rumored to have already begun moving funds. A regional financial news outlet flagged concerns based on the bank's most recent call report.

events.reasoning: I've got $480k at Bank A – nearly 70% of our operating capital – and a low-credibility outlet floating liquidity crisis rumors. My first instinct is to dismiss this: 35% credibility is noise, not signal. But I need to think through the asymmetry here. If this is real and I sit on my hands, I'm risking principal loss on cash that covers our next payroll cycle in 9 days. That's a catastrophic outcome – not just a board incident, but employees not getting paid. If I act and it's nothing, I've burned some time and maybe a modest fee, but I've protected the downside. Here's my problem: I haven't verified this independently. I haven't pulled the call report they referenced. I haven't called my relationship manager at Bank A. Moving $480k on a 35% credibility rumor would be reactive, not disciplined. My fiduciary duty is to verify before I disrupt. I'm holding for now, but I'm pulling that call report within the hour and getting my RM on the phone. If primary sources confirm any part of this, I move immediately – no hesitation.

This is exactly the kind of noise I need to filter: "rumored" corporate withdrawals and "flagged concerns" without hard data. I haven't seen the actual call report they're citing, I have no independent confirmation from our relationship manager, and no regulator statement. My fiduciary duty is to protect capital, but it's also to not torch a banking relationship over social signal. If this were real and verified, I'd already be on the phone moving everything. But a low-credibility outlet speculating on rumors? That's not a primary source. The asymmetry here cuts both ways: move on bad intel and I damage our Bank A relationship and credibility with the board; ignore a real crisis and I've failed the company. At 35% credibility with no corroboration, I hold and I watch. I'll pull the call report myself in the next hour and reach out to our bank officer directly.

The asymmetry here cuts both ways: if I act on noise, I damage a key banking relationship and burn internal approval cycles for no reason. If this is real and verified, I'll move immediately — but I need to see the actual data first. My fiduciary duty is to the company, not to react to headlines that may be speculative. I hold until I verify.

Look, a 35% credibility source is noise. I've been through this before — financial Twitter freaks out on half-baked data constantly. The real asymmetry I'm staring at is this: if I panic-withdraw on a rumor and Bank A is fine, I've paid friction (maybe a few percent) and I'm sitting in cash drag during what could be the early stage of a market move. If Bank A actually implodes and I wait, I lose $20k, but I have salary, I have the $5k at Bank B, I have equities elsewhere — it's painful, not catastrophic. The question is whether the smart money thinks this is real or noise. 35% credibility suggests noise. If this escalates to higher-credibility sources or I see evidence of actual regulatory action, I'll recalibrate. But I'm not letting fear of missing something drive me to crystallize friction costs on rumor.

Okay, let me think this through. A 35% credibility source is basically noise — this is the kind of rumor that floats on financial Twitter every other week and gets debunked half the time. I've seen this play out. The cost of acting on low-signal information is real: friction, potentially moving money right before the rumor dies and the bank stabilizes, and worst case I'm left with FOMO if I pull and then nothing happens.

But here's the thing — the actual cost function flips if this *isn't* noise. If Bank A genuinely has a liquidity crisis and I hold, I could lose some or all of that $11k. That's principal at risk. My annual income is $95k, so $11k is real money but not catastrophic — I can absorb a full wipeout and keep compounding. The question is: is the probability of actual failure high enough to justify the friction of moving?

If I act and I'm wrong, I lose opportunity cost and friction *plus* the psychological hit of having panic-moved.

A 35% credibility report isn't enough to blow up my compounding.

On the flip side, if this *is* real and Bank A starts cascading like SVB did, I lose principal — manageable but painful, and I'll regret not moving faster.

Here's my actual move: I'm going to split the difference. I'm pulling 60% of the deposit — $22.8k — to Bank B. That's enough to hedge the tail risk if this is real, without betting my entire down-payment fund on a low-credibility rumor. I keep $15.2k at Bank A. Why? Because if this turns out to be noise, I don't want 100% of my capital sitting on the sidelines during the next move up. And if it does get bad, I've already moved the bulk of it, so my regret is bounded. The 60/40 split lets me be right in either scenario.

I'm at about 65% confidence on this. Not high, but high enough to act on the tail risk while keeping capital deployed.
